facts.title: Named From Charcoal
facts.text: The word carbon comes from the Latin "carbo," meaning charcoal or ember. Humans have used carbon in the form of soot and charcoal for tens of thousands of years, making it one of the few elements known since prehistoric times. It was first recognized as a true chemical element by Antoine Lavoisier in the 1770s, who proved that diamond is made of pure carbon by burning it.

facts.title: Same Atom, Many Faces
facts.text: Carbon exists as several allotropes built from identical atoms but with wildly different properties. Diamond is the hardest natural material because each carbon bonds to four others in a rigid 3D lattice, while graphite is soft and slippery because it stacks in flat sheets. Other forms include buckyballs (C60), nanotubes, and graphene, a one-atom-thick sheet 200 times stronger than steel.

facts.title: The Backbone Of Life
facts.text: Every known living thing is built on carbon, which is why biology is called "carbon-based." A single carbon atom can form four stable bonds, letting it link into long chains, rings, and branched structures that store information and energy. This versatility creates the proteins, fats, sugars, and DNA that make life possible.

facts.title: It Won't Melt Easily
facts.text: Carbon does not melt under normal pressure; instead it sublimes, turning straight from solid to gas at around 3,650 degrees Celsius. This gives it one of the highest sublimation points of any element. Because of this extreme heat tolerance, carbon is used in rocket nozzles, brake discs, and the heat shields that protect spacecraft during re-entry.

facts.title: A Nuclear Clock
facts.text: A rare radioactive form, carbon-14, forms when cosmic rays strike nitrogen in the upper atmosphere. Living things absorb it constantly, but after death it decays with a half-life of about 5,730 years. By measuring how much carbon-14 remains, scientists can date wood, bone, and cloth up to roughly 50,000 years old, a technique Willard Libby won the 1960 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for inventing.

facts.title: Forged Inside Stars
facts.text: Almost all carbon in the universe is made deep inside dying stars through the triple-alpha process, where three helium nuclei fuse together. When those stars shed their outer layers or explode, they scatter carbon across space to form planets and, eventually, people. As astronomer Carl Sagan put it, we are quite literally made of stardust.

facts.title: The Fourth Most Abundant
facts.text: By mass, carbon is the fourth most abundant element in the universe, after hydrogen, helium, and oxygen. On Earth it cycles constantly between the atmosphere, oceans, rocks, and living things through the carbon cycle. Vast amounts are locked in limestone and chalk, which are largely the calcium carbonate skeletons of ancient sea creatures.

facts.title: Master Of Compounds
facts.text: Carbon forms more compounds than all other elements combined, with well over ten million known and counting. This entire field is called organic chemistry, even though many of these molecules are made in labs and have nothing to do with living things. From plastics and medicines to fuels and dyes, carbon chemistry underpins much of the modern world.

facts.title: Diamonds Are Forever Old
facts.text: Natural diamonds form roughly 150 to 200 kilometers below the surface, where intense heat and pressure squeeze carbon into its hardest crystal form. Many are over a billion years old and are carried upward by rare volcanic eruptions through rock called kimberlite. Despite their value, diamond and humble pencil graphite are chemically the very same element.

facts.title: Carbon In Steel And Air
facts.text: Adding just a fraction of a percent of carbon to iron creates steel, the alloy that built skyscrapers, bridges, and railways. In the air, carbon travels as carbon dioxide, the gas plants breathe in for photosynthesis and the one driving modern climate change. Activated carbon, riddled with microscopic pores, is also used to purify water and filter air because of its enormous surface area.
